name: Linear Search

complexity.time: O(n)
complexity.notes: Baseline — no preconditions on input order.

short_note: Scan elements one by one until the target is found; the floor against which every other search is compared.

name: Binary Search

complexity.time: O(log n)
complexity.notes: Requires the input to be sorted (or monotonic over the answer space).

short_note: Halve the search range each step using a monotone predicate; foundation for 'binary search on the answer' problems.

name: Hash Table

complexity.time: O(1) average for insert/lookup/delete
complexity.notes: Worst case O(n) on adversarial inputs; resolved by either open addressing (linear/quadratic probing, double hashing) or separate chaining.

short_note: Maps keys to slots via a hash function; the workhorse behind nearly every O(n) interview solution that beats a naive O(n log n) sort-based one.

name: Bubble Sort

complexity.time: O(n²) worst & average, O(n) best with early-exit
complexity.notes: Stable; in-place.

short_note: Repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order pairs; the canonical first-sort to teach (and almost never to use).

name: Insertion Sort

complexity.time: O(n²) worst, O(n) on nearly-sorted input
complexity.notes: Stable; in-place; adaptive — the go-to sort for tiny (n ≤ 20) or nearly-sorted arrays.

short_note: Grow a sorted prefix by inserting the next element into its correct position; the engine inside small-array sort fallbacks (e.g. TimSort).

name: Selection Sort

complexity.time: O(n²) all cases
complexity.notes: Not stable. Distinguishing trait: always exactly n−1 swaps — useful when writes are expensive.

short_note: Repeatedly select the minimum of the remaining suffix and swap it into place; the minimum-write counterpart to bubble/insertion.

name: MergeSort

complexity.time: O(n log n) all cases
complexity.space: O(n) auxiliary; O(log n) for linked-list variant
complexity.notes: Stable; the canonical divide-and-conquer sort and the foundation for external sorting.

short_note: Recursively split, sort halves, merge — the canonical D&C sort and the engine behind 'count inversions' and merge-of-k-streams problems.

name: QuickSort

complexity.time: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst
complexity.space: O(log n) stack with median-of-three or randomised pivot
complexity.notes: Not stable. Randomised pivot is the standard defence against O(n²) adversarial inputs.

short_note: Pick a pivot, partition around it (Lomuto or Hoare), recurse on each side; the in-place D&C sort and the parent of QuickSelect.

name: HeapSort

complexity.time: O(n log n) all cases; O(n) build-heap
complexity.notes: Not stable. The only comparison sort that is both in-place AND worst-case O(n log n).

short_note: Build a max-heap in O(n), then repeatedly swap the root with the last element and sift down — in-place and worst-case optimal.

name: Counting Sort

complexity.time: O(n + k) where k is the value range
complexity.notes: Stable; not in-place. Only applies when keys are small integers (or fit a bounded alphabet).

short_note: Tally each key's frequency, then write each key out 'count' times — the canonical linear-time non-comparison sort and the building block of Radix Sort.

name: Radix Sort

complexity.time: O(d × (n + b)) where d = #digits, b = base
complexity.notes: LSD (least-significant-digit) variant is standard for integers; MSD for strings.

short_note: Apply counting-sort digit by digit (LSD or MSD); beats O(n log n) for fixed-width integers and short strings.

name: Bucket Sort

complexity.time: O(n) average for uniformly distributed keys; O(n²) worst
complexity.notes: Distribute keys into b buckets, sort each bucket (often insertion sort), concatenate. Assumes input is uniformly distributed over the bucket range.

short_note: Distribute keys into buckets by range, sort each bucket, concatenate; the workhorse behind the bucketing trick for 'top-k frequent' in O(n).

name: Interpolation Search

complexity.time: O(log log n) on uniformly distributed sorted data; O(n) worst on skewed data
complexity.notes: Variant of binary search that estimates the position via linear interpolation rather than always splitting at the midpoint.

short_note: Binary search where the probe position is estimated from the value distribution; faster than BS on uniform keys, but degenerate on skewed ones.

name: Breadth-First Search (BFS)

complexity.time: O(V + E)
complexity.notes: Yields shortest-path distance in unit-weight graphs.

short_note: Level-by-level exploration using a queue; the primer for every BFS/shortest-path-in-grid/state-space-search problem.

name: Depth-First Search (DFS)

complexity.time: O(V + E)
complexity.notes: Yields entry/exit timestamps used by topo-sort and SCC algorithms.

short_note: Recurse (or explicit stack) into one branch as deep as possible before backtracking; the engine behind island-counting, cycle detection, and topo sort.

name: Topological Sort

complexity.time: O(V + E)
complexity.notes: Only defined on DAGs — cycle ⇒ no valid topological order.

short_note: Order a DAG so every edge points forward; two flavours — Kahn's (BFS over in-degree-0 nodes) and DFS post-order reversal.

name: Dijkstra's Algorithm

complexity.time: O((V + E) log V) with binary heap; O(E + V log V) with Fibonacci heap
complexity.notes: Requires non-negative edge weights.

short_note: Greedy shortest-path with a min-heap; relax outgoing edges of the closest unsettled vertex — the universal non-negative-edge SSSP.

name: Bellman-Ford Algorithm

complexity.time: O(V × E)
complexity.notes: Handles negative edges and detects negative-weight cycles in one extra pass.

short_note: V−1 rounds of relaxing every edge; slower than Dijkstra but correct in the presence of negative edges.

name: A* Algorithm

complexity.time: O(E) with admissible heuristic and consistent priorities
complexity.notes: Optimal when the heuristic is admissible (never overestimates) and monotonically consistent.

short_note: Heuristic-guided Dijkstra: priority key is g(n) + h(n) where h estimates remaining cost; the workhorse of pathfinding in games and robotics.

name: Kruskal's Algorithm

complexity.time: O(E log E) dominated by edge sort
complexity.notes: Sort edges ascending; greedily add each edge whose endpoints are not yet connected (DSU).

short_note: MST via sorted edges + Union-Find: add each edge if it joins two different components; classic greedy + DSU pairing.

name: Prim's Algorithm

complexity.time: O((V + E) log V) with binary heap; O(E + V log V) with Fibonacci heap
complexity.notes: Better than Kruskal on dense graphs; symmetric to Dijkstra in structure.

short_note: Grow the MST one vertex at a time from a seed by extracting the minimum-weight crossing edge from a heap; Dijkstra-shaped.

name: Borůvka's Algorithm

complexity.time: O(E log V)
complexity.notes: Each round contracts the minimum outgoing edge of every component — naturally parallelisable.

short_note: MST via parallel component contraction: in each round, every component picks its cheapest outgoing edge; the historical first MST algorithm (1926).

name: Ford-Fulkerson Method

complexity.time: O(E × max_flow)
complexity.notes: Method, not algorithm — concrete variants (Edmonds-Karp, Dinic) pick a specific augmenting-path strategy.

short_note: Repeatedly find any augmenting path in the residual graph and push flow along it; the foundation of all max-flow algorithms.

name: Edmonds-Karp Algorithm

complexity.time: O(V × E²)
complexity.notes: Ford-Fulkerson with BFS-shortest augmenting paths — guarantees polynomial runtime independent of capacity values.

short_note: Ford-Fulkerson with BFS to choose the shortest augmenting path each round; first polynomial max-flow algorithm.

name: Dinic's Algorithm

complexity.time: O(V² × E); O(E × √V) on unit-capacity graphs (bipartite matching)
complexity.notes: BFS builds a level graph; DFS finds blocking flow; alternation continues until no augmenting path exists.

short_note: Max-flow via alternating BFS level-graph + blocking-flow DFS phases — fast enough for competitive use and bipartite matching.

name: Kosaraju's Algorithm

complexity.time: O(V + E)
complexity.notes: Two DFS passes: one on G to order vertices by finish time, one on G transposed to peel off SCCs.

short_note: Two DFS passes — finish-time order on the original graph, then DFS on the transpose; the most intuitive SCC algorithm.

name: Tarjan's Algorithm

complexity.time: O(V + E)
complexity.notes: Single DFS pass tracking disc[v] (entry index) and low[v] (lowest reachable disc); pops SCCs off a stack as roots are identified.

short_note: Single-pass SCC via DFS with lowlink values; harder to derive than Kosaraju's but only one traversal — also produces articulation points and bridges as variants.

name: Eulerian Path / Circuit

complexity.time: O(V + E)
complexity.notes: Hierholzer's: depth-first walk inserting sub-circuits at vertices with unused edges. Exists iff 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree (undirected) or the standard in/out-degree conditions (directed).

short_note: Walk that uses every edge exactly once; constructed in linear time by Hierholzer's algorithm given the degree precondition.

name: Hamiltonian Path / Cycle

complexity.time: O(2^V × V) via Held-Karp DP; NP-complete in general
complexity.notes: Unlike Eulerian paths, Hamiltonian paths are NP-complete — the bitmask DP works only for small V.

short_note: Visit every VERTEX exactly once (vs Eulerian's every edge); NP-complete in general, solvable for small graphs by bitmask DP.

name: Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS)

complexity.time: O(n²) basic DP; O(n log n) with patience-sort + BS
complexity.notes: The n log n variant uses binary search over a 'tails' array — same as the patience-sorting card-game model.

short_note: Length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence; the canonical 1D DP-with-binary-search problem.

name: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)

complexity.time: O(n × m)
complexity.space: O(n × m); O(min(n,m)) with rolling rows
complexity.notes: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 if s1[i]==s2[j], else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).

short_note: Length of the longest subsequence common to two sequences; the prototypical 2D DP and the foundation of diff/merge tools.

name: Edit Distance (Levenshtein)

complexity.time: O(n × m)
complexity.space: O(n × m); O(min(n,m)) with rolling rows
complexity.notes: Three transitions per cell: insert, delete, replace.

short_note: Minimum insertions, deletions, and substitutions to transform one string into another; the LCS shape with three transitions per cell.

name: 0/1 Knapsack

complexity.time: O(n × W) where W is capacity
complexity.space: O(n × W); O(W) with 1D rolling array
complexity.notes: Pseudo-polynomial — W is part of the input but its magnitude (not bit-length) determines runtime.

short_note: Pick a subset of items (each used 0 or 1 times) maximising value within weight W; the bounded-DP primer underneath subset-sum and partition problems.

name: Subset Sum

complexity.time: O(n × T) where T is target sum
complexity.notes: Boolean specialisation of 0/1 knapsack: dp[t] = whether sum t is achievable.

short_note: Decide whether a subset sums to a target; the 0/1-knapsack shape reduced to a boolean — the engine behind partition-equality and target-sum problems.

name: Rod Cutting

complexity.time: O(n²)
complexity.notes: Unbounded knapsack variant — each cut length is reusable.

short_note: Maximise revenue from cutting a length-n rod into integer-length pieces with a price table; the unbounded-knapsack primer.

name: Matrix Chain Multiplication

complexity.time: O(n³)
complexity.notes: Interval DP: dp[i][j] = min over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + cost(i,k,j).

short_note: Minimise the number of scalar multiplications needed to compute A1·A2·…·An; the prototypical interval-DP problem.

name: Floyd-Warshall Algorithm

complexity.time: O(V³)
complexity.notes: Handles negative edges (no negative cycles). Outperforms running Dijkstra V times on dense graphs and is dramatically simpler to code.

short_note: All-pairs shortest paths via a triple loop: dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + dp[k][j]); 6 lines of code, O(V³).

name: Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP)

complexity.time: O(2^V × V²) Held-Karp DP
complexity.notes: NP-hard in general; exact DP feasible up to V ≈ 20. Branch-and-bound and approximation algorithms exist for larger inputs.

short_note: Visit every city exactly once at minimum cost; the canonical bitmask-DP capstone and an exact algorithm for the Hamiltonian-path family at small V.

name: Bell Numbers and Catalan Numbers

complexity.time: O(n²) Bell triangle; O(n) Catalan from closed form
complexity.notes: Catalan(n) = C(2n,n)/(n+1). Bell(n) counts set partitions; Catalan(n) counts balanced parentheses, BSTs, triangulations, and Dyck paths.

short_note: Two combinatorial recurrences that show up across counting problems — Bell for set partitions, Catalan for balanced structures.

name: Naive String Matching

complexity.time: O(n × m) worst
complexity.notes: Brute force — try every alignment. The baseline against which KMP/RK/BM are compared.

short_note: Try every starting position in the text and compare character by character; the brute-force baseline.

name: Rabin-Karp Algorithm

complexity.time: O(n + m) average with a good hash; O(n × m) worst on adversarial inputs
complexity.notes: Uses a rolling polynomial hash; collisions force fallback to a full character compare.

short_note: Rolling polynomial hash makes the inner comparison O(1) amortised — excellent for multi-pattern search and substring deduplication.

name: Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) Algorithm

complexity.time: O(n + m)
complexity.notes: Builds an array f[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix; used to skip futile re-comparisons in the text.

short_note: Precompute the pattern's failure function so the text pointer never moves backward; the canonical linear-time string matcher.

name: Z Algorithm

complexity.time: O(n)
complexity.notes: Z[i] = length of the longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix of the string. After concatenating pattern + sentinel + text, any Z[i] ≥ |pattern| is a match.

short_note: Build the Z-array in linear time; the simplest exact string matcher to derive from scratch and a Swiss-army knife for prefix-related queries.
references: Gusfield 1997, 'Algorithms on Strings, Trees and Sequences'

name: Boyer-Moore Algorithm

complexity.time: O(n / m) best — sublinear; O(n × m) worst (Boyer-Moore-Horspool variant fixes some pathological cases)
complexity.space: O(σ + m) for the two heuristic tables
complexity.notes: Two precomputed heuristics — bad-character (skip forward to align the mismatched text char) and good-suffix (skip forward to reuse the matched suffix). Used in the GNU grep family.

short_note: Scan the pattern right-to-left and use bad-character + good-suffix heuristics to skip large chunks of the text; sublinear on typical English text.

name: Suffix Array

complexity.time: O(n log n) construction (DC3 is O(n)); O(m log n) substring search
complexity.notes: Combined with the LCP array, supports a wide range of substring queries in logarithmic time.

short_note: Sorted array of all suffixes' start indices; the lighter, space-efficient cousin of the suffix tree and the substring-search workhorse of bioinformatics.

name: Suffix Tree

complexity.time: O(n) construction via Ukkonen's online algorithm
complexity.space: O(n) but with a large constant (~20n bytes)
complexity.notes: Compressed trie of every suffix of the string. Supports many substring queries in O(m); largely supplanted by suffix arrays in practice due to space overhead.

short_note: Compressed trie of all suffixes; supports a vast family of substring queries in linear time but is memory-heavy — suffix arrays + LCP have largely replaced it in practice.

name: Aho-Corasick Algorithm

complexity.time: O(n + m + z) where n = text, m = total pattern length, z = #matches
complexity.notes: Extends KMP to multiple patterns by building a trie + failure links; the engine behind multi-keyword text searchers like fgrep.

short_note: Multi-pattern string matching via a trie augmented with failure links (KMP generalised to many patterns); the canonical 'find any of these N strings in this text' algorithm.

name: Sweep Line Algorithm

complexity.time: O(n log n) due to event-queue sort
complexity.notes: General framework: sort events by x-coordinate; maintain a status structure (often a BST) of active objects and process each event in order.

short_note: Move a vertical line left-to-right, processing discrete events (starts, ends, intersections) while maintaining a status structure — the geometric analogue of a priority queue.
references: de Berg et al., 'Computational Geometry' Ch 2

name: Line Segment Intersection (Bentley-Ottmann)

complexity.time: O((n + k) log n) where k = number of intersections
complexity.notes: Shamos-Hoey (O(n log n)) only reports yes/no; Bentley-Ottmann reports all k intersections.

short_note: Find all intersections among n line segments by sweeping left-to-right and maintaining the vertical order of active segments in a BST.

name: Closest Pair of Points

complexity.time: O(n log n)
complexity.notes: Divide-and-conquer: split at median x, recurse on both halves (getting δ = min(δL, δR)), then check the 2δ-wide strip. The strip check is O(n) because each point has at most 7 neighbours in the strip.

short_note: Find the two nearest points in a set using divide-and-conquer; the classic proof that the strip check has O(1) neighbours per point is the key insight.

name: Graham's Scan (Convex Hull)

complexity.time: O(n log n) dominated by the angular sort
complexity.notes: After sorting by polar angle from the lowest point, process points maintaining a stack — pop while the last three points make a right turn.

short_note: Sort by polar angle and sweep once, using a stack to discard right-turns; the O(n log n) algorithm that establishes the convex-hull lower bound.

name: Jarvis March (Gift Wrapping)

complexity.time: O(n × h) where h = hull vertices — output-sensitive; O(n²) worst
complexity.notes: For small h (sparse hulls) this beats Graham's O(n log n). Chan's algorithm achieves O(n log h) in the worst case.

short_note: Start at the leftmost point and repeatedly pick the point that makes the smallest counter-clockwise angle — output-sensitive and O(n × h).

name: Rotating Calipers

complexity.time: O(n) after O(n log n) hull construction
complexity.notes: Rotates two parallel supporting lines (calipers) around the hull; each rotation step is O(1) via cross-product comparison.

short_note: Rotate a pair of supporting lines around a convex hull to solve diameter, width, and closest-point queries in O(n) after hull construction.

name: Voronoi Diagram

complexity.time: O(n log n) via Fortune's sweep-line
complexity.notes: Naïve incremental is O(n²). Fortune's beach-line sweep achieves the O(n log n) lower bound.

short_note: Partition the plane into regions nearest to each site; the dual of the Delaunay triangulation and the spatial-subdivision backbone behind nearest-neighbour and facility-location problems.

name: Delaunay Triangulation

complexity.time: O(n log n) expected via randomised incremental
complexity.notes: Maximises the minimum angle of all triangles; constructed as the geometric dual of the Voronoi diagram.

short_note: The triangulation of a point set that maximises the minimum triangle angle; the dual of the Voronoi diagram and the mesh-generation primitive.

name: Newton-Raphson Method

complexity.time: O(k) iterations, each O(1) for simple functions
complexity.notes: Quadratically convergent near a root (number of correct digits roughly doubles per step) when f'(x) ≠ 0 and the initial guess is close enough.

short_note: Root-finding via iterated tangent-line extrapolation: x_{n+1} = x_n − f(x_n)/f'(x_n); quadratic convergence makes it the fastest single-root finder in practice.

name: Gradient Descent

complexity.time: O(k × n) per epoch for batch; O(k) per step for SGD
complexity.notes: Learning rate choice is critical — too large diverges, too small converges slowly. Variants: momentum, RMSProp, Adam.

short_note: Iteratively step in the direction of steepest descent (−∇f); the universal first-order optimiser underlying nearly all ML training.
references: Ruder 2016, 'An Overview of Gradient Descent Optimisation Algorithms'

name: Simulated Annealing

complexity.time: O(k) iterations — problem-dependent schedule
complexity.notes: Accepts worse solutions with probability exp(−ΔE/T); temperature T decays by a cooling schedule (geometric, linear, logarithmic). Provably converges to global optimum with a slow enough schedule.

short_note: Probabilistically accept worse moves to escape local optima — the thermal annealing analogy gives the acceptance probability e^{-ΔE/T} that vanishes as temperature T drops.

name: Genetic Algorithms

complexity.time: O(k × P × F) where k=generations, P=population, F=fitness eval
complexity.space: O(P × L) where L = chromosome length
complexity.notes: No convergence guarantee; schema theorem gives partial theoretical justification. Highly tunable (crossover rate, mutation rate, selection pressure).

short_note: Evolve a population of candidate solutions via selection, crossover, and mutation — biologically inspired metaheuristic for black-box optimisation.
references: Holland 1975, 'Adaptation in Natural and Artificial Systems'

name: Simplex Method (Linear Programming)

complexity.time: Exponential worst case; polynomial average case; Klee-Minty shows O(2^n) worst
complexity.notes: Despite worst-case exponential complexity, simplex is fastest in practice. Ellipsoid method (Khachiyan 1979) and interior-point methods (Karmarkar 1984) are polynomial.

short_note: Walk the vertices of a convex polytope (feasible region) following improving edges until the optimum is reached; the dominant LP solver in practice despite exponential worst-case.

name: Interior-Point Method (Barrier Method)

complexity.time: O(n^{3.5} L) where L = input bit-length — polynomial
complexity.notes: Traverses the interior of the feasible polytope rather than its vertices. Modern implementations (IPM solvers like MOSEK, Gurobi) dominate on large dense LPs.

short_note: Traverse the interior of the feasible polytope using barrier functions — polynomial time LP and the theory that settled the complexity of linear programming.

name: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)

complexity.time: O(n × m) basic DP; O(n) with Sakoe-Chiba band constraint
complexity.notes: FastDTW approximation runs in O(n) with configurable radius. Used heavily in time-series classification, speech recognition, and gesture matching.

short_note: Align two temporal sequences by elastically warping the time axis to minimise total point-to-point distance; the time-series analogue of edit distance.

name: Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)

complexity.time: O(n log n)
complexity.notes: Cooley-Tukey radix-2 requires n = power of 2 (zero-pad otherwise). Number-theoretic transform (NTT) avoids floating-point error. FFT-based polynomial multiplication is the engine behind large-integer multiplication (Schönhage-Strassen).

short_note: Evaluate a degree-n polynomial at all nth roots of unity in O(n log n) by recursive halving; the algorithm behind signal processing, image compression, and fast polynomial multiplication.

name: Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find)

complexity.time: O(α(n)) amortised per operation with union-by-rank + path compression
complexity.notes: α is the inverse Ackermann function — effectively constant for all practical n. Without path compression, O(log n) per op.

short_note: Two arrays (parent + rank) supporting near-O(1) merge and find — the backbone of Kruskal's MST and cycle detection in undirected graphs.

name: Trie (Prefix Tree)

complexity.time: O(m) insert/search/delete where m = key length
complexity.space: O(ALPHABET × N × m) worst; compressed tries (Patricia/Radix) reduce this
complexity.notes: Outperforms hashing for prefix queries and lexicographic ordering. Children stored as array[26] or HashMap depending on alphabet size.

short_note: Tree where each edge is a character and nodes mark shared prefixes — O(m) insert/search and instant prefix enumeration without hashing.

name: Ternary Search Tree (TST)

complexity.time: O(m) average; O(m log n) worst
complexity.space: O(n × m) worst — better than trie[26] per node in practice
complexity.notes: Each node has three children: less-than, equal, greater-than. More memory-efficient than a 26-child trie for sparse alphabets.

short_note: Combine BST ordering with trie prefix sharing — three children per node keep memory low while preserving O(m) search; the compact alternative to a fixed-alphabet trie.

name: Binary Search Tree (BST)

complexity.time: O(h) search/insert/delete where h = height; O(log n) balanced, O(n) degenerate
complexity.notes: In-order traversal yields sorted order. Without balancing, degenerate input (sorted insertions) gives O(n) ops. Self-balancing variants (AVL, RB) fix this.

short_note: Binary tree maintaining the BST invariant (left < node < right) — O(log n) when balanced; the conceptual foundation for all ordered-set data structures.

name: AVL Tree

complexity.time: O(log n) search/insert/delete — strictly height-balanced (|h_L − h_R| ≤ 1)
complexity.notes: Height ≤ 1.44 log₂ n. More rotations than red-black on insert/delete (up to O(log n) vs O(1) amortised for RB). Faster lookups in read-heavy workloads.

short_note: Self-balancing BST with a height invariant (|left_h − right_h| ≤ 1) enforced by single and double rotations; the first self-balancing tree and the fastest for lookup-heavy workloads.

name: Red-Black Tree

complexity.time: O(log n) search/insert/delete
complexity.notes: Height ≤ 2 log₂(n+1). At most 2 rotations on insert, at most 3 on delete. Amortised O(1) structural changes per operation — better write throughput than AVL.

short_note: Four colour invariants keep height ≤ 2 log n with O(1) amortised rotations per mutation — the balanced BST in C++ std::map, Java TreeMap, and Linux scheduler (CFS).

name: Splay Tree

complexity.time: O(log n) amortised per operation; O(n) worst-case single op
complexity.notes: Splaying moves the accessed node to the root via zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations. Has the working-set property: recently accessed elements are near the root.

short_note: Self-adjusting BST that splays (moves) every accessed node to the root — O(log n) amortised and naturally cache-friendly for skewed access patterns.

name: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)

complexity.time: O(log n) point update and prefix-sum query
complexity.notes: Uses the lowest-set-bit trick: i += i & (-i) to move to the next responsible cell; i -= i & (-i) to move to the parent. Simpler and faster constant than segment tree for purely prefix-sum queries.

short_note: Store partial sums in an array indexed by the lowest set bit — O(log n) prefix sums and point updates in ~5 lines of code; the lightweight alternative to a segment tree.

name: Segment Tree

complexity.time: O(log n) point update and range query; O(log n) range update with lazy propagation
complexity.notes: 4n array suffices. Lazy propagation defers range updates — each node stores a 'pending' tag flushed on descent. Supports any associative merge operation (sum, min, max, GCD, XOR).

short_note: Divide the array recursively into halves; each node stores the aggregate of its range — any associative query or range update in O(log n) via lazy propagation.
references: Competitive Programming 3 by Steven Halim, Ch 2

name: Bloom Filter

complexity.time: O(k) insert and lookup where k = number of hash functions
complexity.space: O(m) bits — typically m ≈ 10n for 1% FP rate
complexity.notes: False positives possible, false negatives impossible. Optimal k = (m/n) × ln 2. Counting Bloom filter supports deletion at 3–4× space cost.

short_note: A bit-array plus k hash functions: set k bits on insert, query checks all k bits — probabilistic membership with zero false negatives and tunable false-positive rate.

name: Skip List

complexity.time: O(log n) expected search/insert/delete
complexity.space: O(n log n) expected due to multiple levels
complexity.notes: Each element appears at each level with probability p (typically ½). Expected height = log_{1/p} n. Used in Redis sorted sets and LevelDB skip-list memtable.

short_note: Layered linked lists with exponentially sparser express lanes — O(log n) expected ops with simpler concurrent implementation than balanced BSTs.

name: Graph Coloring

complexity.time: O(V + E) greedy; optimal coloring is NP-complete
complexity.notes: Greedy gives χ ≤ Δ+1 (Δ = max degree). Brooks' theorem: χ ≤ Δ for any graph that is neither an odd cycle nor a complete graph. Used in register allocation and exam scheduling.

short_note: Assign colours to vertices so no two adjacent vertices share a colour; greedy approximation runs in O(V+E) but optimal colouring is NP-complete.

name: Bipartite Matching (Hopcroft-Karp)

complexity.time: O(E √V) Hopcroft-Karp; O(VE) augmenting-path (Ford-Fulkerson on bipartite graph)
complexity.notes: Hopcroft-Karp finds all shortest augmenting paths in a single BFS phase, then augments them together — √V phases suffice.

short_note: Find the maximum matching in a bipartite graph; Hopcroft-Karp achieves O(E √V) by augmenting along all shortest paths simultaneously.

name: PageRank Algorithm

complexity.time: O(k × (V + E)) for k power-iteration steps until convergence
complexity.notes: Converges geometrically; k ≈ 50–100 iterations suffices in practice. Teleportation factor d ≈ 0.85 prevents rank sinks and ensures the Markov chain is ergodic.

short_note: Model a random surfer who follows links with probability d and teleports with probability 1-d; the stationary distribution of this Markov chain is the PageRank vector.

name: Spectral Graph Theory

complexity.time: O(V³) for full eigendecomposition; O(k × V × E) for k leading eigenvectors via power iteration
complexity.notes: Fiedler vector (second smallest eigenvector of the Laplacian) gives a near-optimal graph bisection. Used in spectral clustering, graph partitioning, and dimensionality reduction.

short_note: Use the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian to reveal community structure, connectivity, and clustering — the mathematical bridge between linear algebra and graph algorithms.

name: Planarity Testing (Kuratowski / Boyer-Myrvold)

complexity.time: O(V + E) — linear time
complexity.notes: Kuratowski's theorem: a graph is planar iff it has no subgraph homeomorphic to K5 or K3,3. Boyer-Myrvold is the cleanest linear-time implementation.

short_note: Determine if a graph can be drawn in the plane without edge crossings in O(V+E); rooted in Kuratowski's characterisation via K5 and K3,3 minors.

name: SHA Hash Family (SHA-1 / SHA-256 / SHA-3)

complexity.time: O(n) where n = message length (block-by-block processing)
complexity.notes: SHA-256: Merkle-Damgård construction with 64-round Davies-Meyer compression. SHA-3 (Keccak): sponge construction — absorb then squeeze.

short_note: Iterative block-by-block compression into a fixed-size digest; SHA-256's Merkle-Damgård construction versus SHA-3's sponge construction is the key architectural contrast.

name: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard)

complexity.time: O(1) per block (10/12/14 rounds of byte operations on a 4×4 state matrix)
complexity.notes: Key schedule expands the 128/192/256-bit key into 11/13/15 round keys. Hardware AES-NI instructions reduce encryption to ~1 cycle per byte on modern CPUs.

short_note: Substitution-permutation network operating on a 4×4 byte state matrix through SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, and AddRoundKey — the universal symmetric cipher.

name: DES / 3DES

complexity.time: O(1) per 64-bit block (16 Feistel rounds)
complexity.notes: 56-bit effective key is brute-forceable; broken in 1998 by EFF DES Cracker in 56 hours. 3DES triples the key length at 3× the cost; replaced by AES (NIST 2002).

short_note: The 16-round Feistel cipher that defined symmetric encryption; historically important but insecure at 56-bit key length — study as the contrast to AES's SPN structure.

name: Merkle Tree

complexity.time: O(n) build; O(log n) proof generation and verification
complexity.notes: Leaf nodes store H(data); internal nodes store H(left_child ∥ right_child). Tamper-evident: changing one leaf invalidates O(log n) hashes up to the root.

short_note: Binary tree of hashes where each parent = H(left∥right); changing any leaf invalidates O(log n) hashes — the tamper-evidence primitive in git, blockchain, and certificate transparency.

name: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange

complexity.time: O(log p) for modular exponentiation via fast-modular-exp
complexity.notes: Security rests on the discrete logarithm problem in Z_p* (or on an elliptic curve for ECDH). ECDH achieves equivalent security at ~7× shorter key lengths.

short_note: Exchange a shared secret over an insecure channel using the computational hardness of the discrete logarithm: each party computes g^{ab} mod p without ever transmitting ab.

name: RSA Algorithm

complexity.time: O(log e × log² n) encrypt/decrypt via fast-modular-exp on n-bit numbers
complexity.notes: Security rests on integer factorisation hardness. Key generation requires large prime testing (Miller-Rabin). 2048-bit keys standard; 4096-bit for long-term security.

short_note: Encrypt with public key e: C = M^e mod n; decrypt with private key d: M = C^d mod n — security reduces to factoring n = p×q into its two large primes.

name: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC)

complexity.time: O(log k) scalar multiplication on the curve via double-and-add
complexity.notes: 256-bit ECC offers equivalent security to 3072-bit RSA. ECDSA used for digital signatures; ECDH for key exchange; Ed25519 (twisted Edwards curve) is the modern default for SSH keys.

short_note: Perform Diffie-Hellman and RSA on the group of points of an elliptic curve over a finite field — equivalent security at dramatically smaller key sizes.

name: MapReduce

complexity.time: O(n/P) map + O(n log n / P) sort + O(n/P) reduce for P workers — network shuffle dominates in practice
complexity.space: O(n) local per worker; global shuffle data can exceed input size
complexity.notes: Fault tolerance via task re-execution. Combiner reduces shuffle volume. Replaced by Spark DAG execution for iterative workloads.

short_note: Decompose a computation into embarrassingly parallel Map steps and an aggregating Reduce step over a sorted shuffle — the shared-nothing batch-processing model behind Hadoop.

name: Work-Stealing Scheduler

complexity.time: O(T₁/P + T∞) where T₁ = sequential work, T∞ = critical-path length, P = processors
complexity.space: O(P × D) for deques of depth D
complexity.notes: Achieves within a constant factor of optimal work distribution with high probability. Used in Java ForkJoin, Go runtime, Intel TBB, Cilk.

short_note: Each thread has a deque; idle threads steal tasks from the tail of others' deques — achieves near-optimal parallelism with O(P × D) space and provably low steal rate.

name: Bitonic Sort

complexity.time: O(n log² n) comparisons on P = n/2 processors
complexity.notes: Optimal for a sorting network of P processors. AKS network achieves O(log n) depth but with huge constants — Bitonic is the practical choice.

short_note: Merge a bitonic sequence (first increasing then decreasing) in log n parallel steps; the canonical O(n log² n) sorting network for GPU and FPGA implementations.

name: Distributed Hash Table (DHT)

complexity.time: O(log n) hops to route a key to its responsible node
complexity.space: O(log n) routing table entries per node
complexity.notes: Consistent hashing maps keys to a ring; each node is responsible for the arc before it. Adding/removing one node redistributes only O(K/n) keys (vs O(K) for a plain modulo hash).

short_note: Map each key to a node on a consistent-hashing ring so adding or removing a node only remaps O(K/n) keys — the decentralised lookup primitive behind BitTorrent, Cassandra, and Dynamo.

name: Paxos Consensus Algorithm

complexity.time: 2 message round-trips (prepare + accept) per value; latency-bound, not compute-bound
complexity.space: O(n) per acceptor for log storage
complexity.notes: FLP impossibility: no deterministic algorithm can guarantee consensus in an async system with one crash-faulty process. Paxos sidesteps FLP by being safe always but live only when a majority is reachable.

short_note: Reach agreement among n processes tolerating ⌊n/2⌋ failures via two phases — Prepare/Promise and Accept/Accepted — using the highest-numbered proposal as the invariant.

name: Raft Consensus Algorithm

complexity.time: Same as Paxos: 2 RTTs per log entry in steady state
complexity.space: O(log entries) per server for the log
complexity.notes: Raft decomposes consensus into leader election, log replication, and safety. Designed explicitly for understandability — randomised election timeouts avoid split votes.

short_note: Leader-based consensus protocol with randomised election timeouts and a strict log-matching invariant — the same guarantees as Paxos in a structure designed to be taught and implemented.
references: Ongaro & Ousterhout 2014, 'In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm'

name: Activity Selection Problem

complexity.time: O(n log n) for sorting; O(n) greedy scan
complexity.notes: Select maximum number of non-overlapping intervals by always choosing the activity with the earliest finish time. Correctness proved by exchange argument.

short_note: Select the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals by greedily picking the one that finishes earliest — the exchange-argument proof is the canonical greedy correctness template.

name: Huffman Encoding

complexity.time: O(n log n) using a min-heap
complexity.notes: Provably optimal prefix code (Shannon entropy lower bound). Used in DEFLATE (gzip/zlib), JPEG, and MP3.

short_note: Build a min-heap of symbol frequencies and repeatedly merge the two lowest into a new internal node — the resulting binary tree gives the provably optimal variable-length prefix code.

name: Quickselect

complexity.time: O(n) expected, O(n²) worst-case; O(n) worst with median-of-medians pivot
complexity.space: O(1) iterative; O(log n) expected stack for recursive
complexity.notes: The median-of-medians pivot selection guarantees O(n) worst case but has a large constant — typically only used when deterministic O(n) is required.

short_note: Partition around a pivot like Quicksort but recurse only into the half containing the kth element — O(n) expected selection without sorting the full array.

name: Reservoir Sampling

complexity.time: O(n) one-pass over stream; O(k log(n/k)) with Algorithm Z for large streams
complexity.notes: Each element i ≥ k is included with probability k/i; when included, it replaces a uniformly random reservoir entry. Mathematically guarantees a uniform random sample without knowing n in advance.

short_note: Maintain a size-k reservoir and accept each incoming stream element with probability k/i — guarantees a uniform random sample from a stream of unknown length in one pass.

name: Karatsuba Algorithm

complexity.space: O(n log n) due to recursion and temporaries
complexity.notes: Reduces n-digit multiplication from 4 recursive half-multiplications to 3 via the identity ac + bd + (a+b)(c+d) - ac - bd. Used in Python's big-integer multiply for large numbers.

short_note: Multiply two n-digit numbers with 3 (instead of 4) half-size multiplications via the identity that expresses the cross term from the sum — the prototype of the divide-and-conquer 'algebraic trick'.

name: Strassen's Matrix Multiplication

complexity.notes: Reduces the 8 multiplications of naive block-MM to 7 via algebraic identities — same divide-and-conquer trick as Karatsuba. Best known bound (2025) is ~O(n^{2.371}) via laser method. Practical cutoff to naive is n ≈ 64.

short_note: Multiply two n×n matrices with 7 (instead of 8) n/2 × n/2 submatrix products via Strassen's seven identities — the recursive divide-and-conquer answer to 'can we beat O(n³)?'

name: Monte Carlo Method

complexity.time: O(k) samples — error ∝ 1/√k (central limit theorem)
complexity.notes: Variance reduction techniques (importance sampling, stratified sampling, MCMC) improve the 1/√k convergence rate. Used in numerical integration, option pricing, and physics simulation.

short_note: Estimate a quantity by averaging over many random trials — the 1/√k convergence from the CLT is the universal cost model, and the key design decision is how to draw samples efficiently.

name: Backtracking

complexity.time: O(b^d) in the worst case where b = branching factor and d = solution depth; pruning can give enormous practical speedups
complexity.notes: Constraint propagation (arc consistency, forward checking) dramatically reduces the effective branching factor. The backbone of constraint-satisfaction solvers (Sudoku, N-Queens, SAT solvers).

short_note: Explore the solution space depth-first, pruning branches the moment a constraint is violated — exponential worst-case but often dramatically faster in practice with good pruning.

name: Smith-Waterman Algorithm

complexity.time: O(n × m) — same as LCS/edit-distance DP
complexity.space: O(n × m); O(n) with traceback tricks
complexity.notes: Local alignment: reset to 0 when the score goes negative — finds the best matching sub-sequence rather than requiring full-length alignment. GPU-accelerated in BLAST.

short_note: Local sequence alignment via DP with a reset-to-zero clause — identifies the best matching sub-region between two sequences regardless of flanking noise.

name: Needleman-Wunsch Algorithm

complexity.time: O(n × m)
complexity.space: O(n × m); linear with Hirschberg's divide-and-conquer
complexity.notes: Global alignment — the score never resets. Gap penalty models: linear (LCS-like) vs affine (separate gap-open and gap-extend costs, solved with 3-state DP).

short_note: Global sequence alignment — edit-distance DP with a biologically meaningful scoring matrix (BLOSUM/PAM) and affine gap penalties instead of uniform substitution costs.

name: Canny Edge Detection

complexity.time: O(n × m) for an n×m image — single pass per stage
complexity.notes: Five stages: Gaussian blur → gradient magnitude/direction → non-maximum suppression → double threshold → edge tracking by hysteresis. Optimal by three criteria: detection, localisation, and single response.

short_note: Five-stage pipeline — blur, gradient, thin, threshold, hysteresis — that provably optimises edge detection, localisation, and the single-response criterion simultaneously.

name: RANSAC (Random Sample Consensus)

complexity.time: O(k × n) where k = iterations; k = log(1-p)/log(1-(1-e)^s) for desired confidence p, outlier fraction e, sample size s
complexity.notes: The dominant robust estimator in computer vision (homography, fundamental matrix, pose estimation). Works when outlier fraction < 50%; degrades gracefully above that.

short_note: Randomly sample the minimum model-fitting set, count inliers, repeat — the robust estimator that tolerates a high fraction of outliers by design.

name: B-Tree

complexity.time: O(log_t n) search/insert/delete where t = branching factor (often 100–1000 on disk)
complexity.notes: Pages hold ⌈t/2⌉ to t-1 keys; splits and merges keep the tree balanced. B+ trees (all data in leaves, internal nodes are index-only) are universal in database engines.

short_note: Generalise the BST to nodes with up to t-1 keys and t children — wide, shallow trees minimise disk I/O; the universal storage structure in databases and file systems.

name: Log-Structured Merge Tree (LSM Tree)

complexity.time: O(1) amortised write (append-only); O(log n) read with Bloom-filter acceleration
complexity.space: O(n) on disk; O(memtable size) in memory
complexity.notes: Write amplification: each byte written once to memory, then compacted multiple times to disk. Read amplification reduced via Bloom filters on each SSTable level. Used in LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra, HBase.

short_note: Accept writes into an in-memory buffer (MemTable); flush sorted runs (SSTables) to disk; merge levels in background — write-optimised at the cost of read and space amplification.

name: TCP Congestion Control (CUBIC / Reno)

complexity.time: O(1) per ACK/NACK event — purely reactive
complexity.notes: Additive-increase / multiplicative-decrease (AIMD) converges to fair allocation via Lyapunov analysis. CUBIC replaces Reno in Linux (2006); BBR (Google 2016) uses bandwidth-delay estimation instead of loss signals.

short_note: Probe available bandwidth with additive increases then halve the window on packet loss (AIMD) — mathematically guaranteed to converge to max-min fair sharing under congestion.

name: Euclidean Algorithm (GCD)

complexity.time: O(log min(a,b)) — Fibonacci inputs are worst case
complexity.notes: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b); base case gcd(a, 0) = a. Lehmer's improvement handles big-integer GCD.

short_note: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) — the oldest non-trivial algorithm (~300 BCE), converges in O(log) steps, and is the foundation of modular arithmetic and RSA key generation.

name: Extended Euclidean Algorithm

complexity.time: O(log min(a,b)) — same as basic GCD
complexity.notes: Returns (g, x, y) such that ax + by = g = gcd(a, b). When gcd(a, m) = 1, x is the modular inverse of a mod m.

short_note: Extend the Euclidean algorithm to return Bézout coefficients (x, y) with ax + by = gcd(a, b) — the direct route to modular inverses and the core of RSA decryption key generation.

name: Modular Multiplicative Inverse

complexity.time: O(log p) via Fermat's little theorem (fast-modular-exp); O(log a) via extended GCD
complexity.notes: By Fermat: a^{-1} ≡ a^{p-2} mod p when p is prime. Extended GCD works for any modulus m with gcd(a,m)=1. Linear sieve method computes inverses for 1…n in O(n).

short_note: Find x such that ax ≡ 1 (mod m) — the divide operation of modular arithmetic, used in RSA, CRT, and combinatorial counting modulo a prime.

name: Sieve of Eratosthenes

complexity.time: O(n log log n) classic; O(n) linear sieve (each composite crossed out exactly once)
complexity.notes: Segmented sieve uses O(√n) space and processes primes up to n in cache-friendly chunks. The linear sieve additionally computes smallest prime factors for factorisation.

short_note: Mark multiples of each prime starting from 2 — the O(n log log n) sieve that generates all primes up to n and is trivially extended to compute totient, divisor count, and smallest prime factors.

name: Fast Modular Exponentiation

complexity.time: O(log e) multiplications for base^e mod m
complexity.notes: Process bits of e from MSB to LSB: square each step, multiply only for 1 bits. Reduce mod m after each operation to keep numbers bounded.

short_note: Square the base and halve the exponent on each step — O(log e) multiplications for base^e mod m, the critical primitive in RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and Miller-Rabin primality.

name: Matrix Exponentiation

complexity.time: O(k³ log n) for k×k matrices raised to power n
complexity.notes: Any linear recurrence of order k can be encoded as a k×k matrix; computing the nth term then costs O(k³ log n). Standard trick: Fibonacci in O(log n) via 2×2 matrix.

short_note: Apply binary exponentiation to square matrices — encodes any linear recurrence in a k×k transfer matrix and evaluates the nth term in O(k³ log n).

name: Karger's Minimum Cut Algorithm

complexity.time: O(V² log³ V) for Karger-Stein with amplification; O(E × V²) naive Karger
complexity.notes: Each single run succeeds with probability ≥ 2/(V(V-1)). Running O(V² log V) times and taking the minimum gives high-probability correctness. Karger-Stein improves to O(V² log³ V) via recursive contraction.

short_note: Randomly contract edges (merging endpoints) until two super-nodes remain — the resulting cut is the global min-cut with probability ≥ 2/V²; the prototype randomised graph algorithm.

name: Vertex Cover 2-Approximation

complexity.time: O(V + E) — one pass over edges
complexity.notes: Repeatedly pick an uncovered edge and include both endpoints. The result is ≤ 2 × OPT (since OPT must contain at least one endpoint of each chosen edge, and the chosen edges form a matching).

short_note: Greedily pick uncovered edges and include both endpoints — the simplest 2-approximation algorithm and the textbook proof that NP-hard problems can admit provably good polynomial approximations.

name: Set Cover Greedy Approximation

complexity.time: O(n × m) where n = universe size, m = number of sets — dominated by coverage tracking
complexity.notes: Approximation ratio = H_n ≈ ln n + 0.577 (harmonic number). This is near-optimal: unless P=NP, no poly-time algorithm achieves (1-ε) ln n approximation.

short_note: Greedily add the set that covers the most uncovered elements — achieves a H(n) ≈ ln n approximation, which is essentially optimal unless P=NP.

name: Q-Learning

complexity.time: O(S × A) per step where S = states, A = actions
complexity.notes: Converges to the optimal Q-function under mild conditions (every state-action visited infinitely often; learning rate schedule satisfies Robbins-Monro). Deep Q-Network (DQN) replaces the table with a neural network.

short_note: Tabular model-free reinforcement learning: update Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ max Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)] — learns the optimal policy without a model of the environment.

name: Deep Q-Networks (DQN)

complexity.time: O(batch × network_layers) per gradient step
complexity.notes: Two key stabilisation tricks: experience replay (breaks temporal correlation) and a target network (fixed weights for the bootstrap target, updated every N steps). Extensions: Double DQN, Dueling DQN, Prioritised Replay.

short_note: Replace the Q-table with a neural network; stabilise training with an experience replay buffer and a target network updated less frequently — the breakthrough that achieved human-level Atari play.

name: Grover's Algorithm

complexity.time: O(√N) oracle queries — quadratic speedup over classical O(N) search
complexity.notes: Proved optimal for unstructured quantum search (no quantum algorithm can do better than O(√N)). Implies AES-128 effectively has 64-bit quantum security (requires 2^64 Grover iterations).

short_note: Quantum amplitude amplification finds a marked item in an unsorted database with O(√N) oracle calls — the quadratic speedup is provably optimal for unstructured search.

name: Shor's Algorithm

complexity.time: O((log N)³) quantum gate operations — polynomial in input size
complexity.notes: Reduces integer factorisation to period-finding, which QFT solves in O(log² N) operations. Would break RSA and Diffie-Hellman if large fault-tolerant quantum computers existed. Post-quantum cryptography (NIST 2024: CRYSTALS-Kyber, CRYSTALS-Dilithium) provides quantum-resistant alternatives.

short_note: Reduce factoring to quantum period-finding via the quantum Fourier transform — polynomial time on a quantum computer, exponential time classically; the algorithm that broke RSA's theoretical foundation.

name: Blockchain Consensus (Proof-of-Work / Proof-of-Stake)

complexity.time: O(1) per block to verify (SHA256); mining difficulty is tuned so blocks arrive at target rate
complexity.space: O(n) for the full chain history — grows indefinitely
complexity.notes: PoW: probabilistic finality — 6 confirmations gives 2^{-6} fork probability at 50% honest hash rate. PoS (Ethereum post-merge): Casper FFG gives economic finality within 2 epochs (~12 min). Energy consumption contrast: PoW (Bitcoin) ~150 TWh/year vs PoS (Ethereum) ~0.01 TWh/year.

short_note: Chain blocks by hashing the previous block header into the new one; require a valid proof-of-work (hash below target) to extend the chain — longest-chain rule resolves forks probabilistically.
